If you're new to anarchism, the first thing to understand is that many self-professed "anarchists" are anything but. For example, they'll insist that, one way or another, "capitalism" "will not be allowed," apparently without even beginning to grasp the fact that any mechanism that would make something "not allowed" is directly contrary to anarchism. As near as I can tell, that's because they're so inured to authoritarianism that they just don't recognize it, and particularly (in typical selfish human fashion) when it's in support of some set of norms that they prefer. As I've had cause to point out often - the common human perception is that when I'm forced to abide by the norms of others, that's tyranny, but when others are forced to abide by my norms, that's justice.

Next - the simplest, though not terribly useful, answer is that many "anarchists" say that anarcho-capitalism is not really anarchism because many "anarchists" say that anarcho-capitalism is not really anarchism. That is to say, it's not that they consider ideas and come to conclusions, but that they memorize and repeat bits of dogma, and "anarcho-capitalism is not really anarchism" is one of those bits of dogma.

Now, that's not to say that there's absolutely no thought behind the idea. The most common basis for the claim, at least from those who go that far, is that capitalism is innately authoritarian, so anarcho-capitalism is self-contradictory.

That gets into a complexity with "capitalism" (and similarly with "communism"). As a general rule, when an opponent of one of the two systems speaks of the system, what s/he is actually referring to is the system as it is generally manifested in the real world, which is to say, the system as it is in authoritarian systems. When an opponent of "capitalism" uses the term, s/he's not referring to the "exchange (of) goods and services based on mutual agreement." S/he's referring to the system that actually exists in nations like the US - the system under which wealth = political power. And the same thing happens (though, since it often involves the same people, sort of in the opposite direction) with "communism" - with the advocates referring to the ideal form and the opponents referring to the common real (and authoritarian) form. So when some argue that "capitalism" is contrary to anarchism (or, as others do, that communism is), what they're really arguing is that the form of those things with which they're familiar, which is to say the form that exists under authoritarian regimes, is contrary to anarchism. That's tritely true, but doesn't say anything really about the economic systems in and of themselves. Self-evidently, ANY system envisioned as it exists under authoritarianism would contradict with a society that's defined by the absence of authoritarianism.

Now, that said, there is one central problem with anarcho-capitalism. In order to work, anarcho-capitalism requires universal agreement to a specific set of property norms, and since humans don't universally agree to anything, it at least implies the existence of some mechanism(s) of authority to enforce compliance with those property norms. And in fact, anarcho-capitalism explicitly advocates for those mechanisms of authority. It pretends to anarchism because one would purportedly "voluntarily" agree to be subject to those norms, but in fact, the "voluntary" part disappears almost immediately.

Example - I'm part of an anarcho-capitalist community. I've agreed to their property norms, which include, among other things, the view that the fruit of a tree that's on a resident's property is, itself, the property of that resident. My neighbor has an apple tree. He believes the apples are his property and I agree that the apples are his property. It's a mutually voluntary arrangement, and all's well and good. However, if Joe Blow, who's not a part of the community, comes wandering in and eats one of my neighbor's apples, he's going to be held liable for taking my neighbor's property, and that in spite of the fact that he did not volunteer to comply with those property norms. And there goes the "anarchism" right there.

And note that all of that, though with different specifics, can be said for anarcho-communism - it too requires compliance with a specific set of property norms.

And... all that said, I have a broader view. I count ALL subdivisions of anarchism (including the one that's just called "anarchism") as something less than actual anarchism, simply because all of them presume universal agreement to one or another specific set of norms. At best, they're hopelessly speculative - taking a wild guess that people, left entirely free to choose, are all going to choose this or that particular form of "anarchism," but more often, they're fundamentally, and often overtly, authoritarian, presuming at some point the right to bring some authority to bear to force compliance with their norms.

To my thinking, anarchism requires exactly one thing and one thing only - the complete and total absence of any and all formalized mechanisms by which the wills of some are imposed upon others - of any and all mechanisms of authority - of any and all "-archisms." There's literally no telling what would come of that. It could only be whatever might arise from all of the wholly unconstrained decisions made by all of the entirely free participants. As far as capitalism and communism go, I would sort of expect something somewhere between the two, with pocket communities of one or the other extreme, just because both seem to have their supporters so both would be things that unconstrained people would choose. But there's really no way of knowing, so presuming one or another is pointlessly speculative at best.

Here's the metaphor. Suppose you had a serious commitment to the mainstream version of Christianity. From that viewpoint you might disagree with non-Trinitarian versions such as the Unitarians, apocalyptic sects such as the Jehovah's Witnesses, or other sects such as the Mormons. A less argumentative mainstream Christian, however, would adopt a laisée faire attitude to such things in the firm confidence that their theologies are simply wrong, that it is pointless to argue with them and that their existence doesn't really affect whatever you and other Christians of your sort might like to do to "bring the truth of Christ" into the world because they are so insignificant in the global context of Christianity. Same thing for those who know what the history of anarchism is, of what it is even now across the world and what are the practical things anarchists can do besides having philosophical arguments.

I know this sounds mean, but I'd like to pose a question here to those who consider themselves 'anarcho-capitalists'. What are the real and practical things that these different types of anarchists could collaborate on ? Perhaps opposition to foreign wars. That would be nice if there existed an organized mass movement against it - which there is not. In the absence of such any 'collaboration' involves nothing beyond agreement on social media and goes nowhere. Drug laws ? Yes, but at least in my view this is of lesser importance and is, in any case, being promoted very effectively by non-anarchist elements. Patent laws maybe ? Once more, however, are there any practical things to do ?

My own version of anarchism involves activity in such 'mass' (sorry about the commie word - call it 'popular' instead) organizations as unions, cooperatives, neighbourhood associations, credit unions and protest movement. No millennium there, but all these groupings have the potential to expand freedom and equality to at least a minimal degree.

I have my own version of what the economy of an anarchist society would look like, basically a mixed economy where popular organizations would prevent the rise of excessive private power, but many things would still remain a matter of a market. That's fine, but it has no effect on what I might do today nor on what I would recommend others do. For example everyone should have access to free shoes (anarchocommunism ?), but for those who wished to follow fashion - and there would still be many, human beings being human beings.
